cases.d: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland; after a pupil's parents complained, the school sent him back to Australia without informing police. He was arrested in Sydney in 2017, extradition was approved in 2019, and in June 2021 he pleaded guilty to two charges involving two boys between 1973 and 1976.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, Fort Augustus Abbey, citing BBC

cases.n: Sodalicio layman arrested with a boy, Lima 2007
cases.who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (consecrated layman)
cases.d: In 2007 Daniel Bernardo Beltrán Murguía Ward, a consecrated layman of the Sodalitium, was found in a Lima hostel photographing an 11-year-old boy; police reported photos of two other boys on his camera. He denied the charges and was removed from the group.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Latin America, citing Peruvian press

nets.reach_note: reach = countries with a case record in this dataset. Abuse findings exist far beyond these; many countries with large Catholic populations have had no national inquiry (see notes).
nets.d: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.
nets.cite: UN CRC Concluding observations on the Holy See, 2014; national inquiry reports listed in cases

nets.reach_note: Documented: Maciel abused seminarians in Spain and Rome; Legion confirmed abuse by Fr William Izquierdo in Ireland and the US; Cancún school case in Mexico. Estimated: countries where the Legion runs institutions; the 2019 report's 175 cases were not broken down by country in sources opened.
nets.d: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.
nets.cite: Legion of Christ report, 21 December 2019; Holy See communiqué 1 May 2010

nets.n: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana)
nets.reach_note: Abuse findings documented in Peru; the group operated in the other listed countries.
nets.d: Lay society founded in Lima in 1971 by Luis Fernando Figari. Exposed by journalists in 2015; investigators found sexual abuse of minors and adults by Figari and others. Figari and over a dozen members were expelled in 2024 and Pope Francis signed its suppression on 14 January 2025.
nets.cite: Holy See decrees 2024–25; Salinas & Ugaz, Mitad monjes, mitad soldados (2015)

nets.reach_note: Documented findings or convictions in Ireland (Ryan, 2024 scoping), Canada (Mount Cashel), Australia (Royal Commission, WA orphanages), UK (St Ninian's Scotland; Northern Ireland convictions), US (2011 bankruptcy and settlement). India: allegations only. Malta: child migrants were sent to Christian Brothers' WA institutions (per inquiries; not detailed in sources opened).
nets.d: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.
nets.cite: Ryan Report 2009; Royal Commission (Australia) 2017; Wikipedia, Congregation of Christian Brothers

nets.reach_note: Peru: Chilean Brother Abel Pérez was transferred there after confessing. Fiji: compensation disparities with NZ reported, not detailed.
nets.d: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

nets.reach_note: Samoa: a priest convicted in Melbourne was allegedly moved there to avoid police. Timor-Leste: Bishop Belo is a Salesian.
nets.d: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.
nets.cite: Wikipedia, Abuse by members of Roman Catholic orders; Salesians of Don Bosco

nets.reach_note: Germany: Canisius-Kolleg 2010; Bolivia: Pedrajas and cover-up by provincial superiors; Spain: Pedrajas was Spanish, and a German Jesuit offended in Spanish and Chilean Jesuit schools; US: cases in several schools (not detailed here).
nets.d: The 2010 Canisius-Kolleg disclosures in Berlin started Germany's abuse reckoning. In 2023 El País published the diary of Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas recording abuse of more than 80 minors in Bolivia, with superiors aware from 1978.
nets.cite: El País, 30 April 2023; Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Germany

nets.n: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
nets.reach_note: Sri Lanka: Bernard McGrath returned from there before arrest; no finding there.
nets.d: Australia's Royal Commission found 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused, the highest of any order. In New Zealand, 21 of 37 Brothers in Christchurch faced allegations over Marylands School and the Hebron Trust.
nets.cite: Royal Commission (Australia) data 2017; NZ Royal Commission 2023

flows.n: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi
flows.d: Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf; Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

flows.n: Chile → Peru: Marist Brother Abel Pérez
flows.d: After confessing to superiors in 2010 that he had abused minors, Brother Abel Pérez was transferred by the Marist Brothers to Peru.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Chile; Marist Brothers

flows.n: Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S.
flows.to: South America (he had also offended in Jesuit schools in Chile and Spain)
flows.d: After he admitted abusing pupils at St. Blasien (1982–84) and Canisius-Kolleg, the Jesuits said his superiors helped him emigrate to South America, where he lived as of 2010. A separate summary says he had also offended in Jesuit schools in Chile and Spain; his exact destination country is not confirmed.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Germany; Abuse by members of Roman Catholic orders

flows.n: Essen → Munich: Fr Peter Hullermann
flows.d: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Ratzinger accepted accused priest Peter Hullermann for therapy; he was then given parish work and abused again, and was convicted in 1986.
flows.cite: Süddeutsche Zeitung 2010 via Wikipedia; Munich report 2022

flows.n: Slovenia → Malawi: Fr Franc Frantar
flows.d: Detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors, Frantar avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary, returning after an Interpol notice.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Europe

flows.n: Lima → Bolivia: Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas
flows.d: Spanish Jesuit Pedrajas settled in Bolivia after his first abuse in Lima in 1964, then abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools there; he confessed to a superior in 1978, who covered it up.
flows.cite: El País, 30 April 2023, via Spanish Wikipedia

flows.n: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
flows.to: Rhode Island, North Dakota and Boston, USA
flows.d: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Brendan Smyth

flows.n: Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson
flows.d: After complaints in the 1980s Robinson was moved to another parish without police being told; he then fled to the US in 1985 and the archdiocese kept paying him for seven years. A BBC team found him in California in 2003; he was extradited and jailed for 21 years.
flows.cite: IICSA, Archdiocese of Birmingham report, 20 June 2019

flows.n: Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore
flows.d: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore, later convicted (2018) of abusing three children and a student priest, to Toronto and to Fort Augustus.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases by country (Scotland)

flows.n: Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander
flows.d: After a pupil's parents complained, the abbey school sent the monk back to Australia without telling police; he was arrested in Sydney in 2017 and pleaded guilty in 2021.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Fort Augustus Abbey

flows.n: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox
flows.d: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating him; he was jailed in 2015.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Australia

flows.n: Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged)
flows.d: A Salesian priest convicted of abuse in Melbourne was allegedly moved to Samoa to avoid further police investigation.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Abuse by members of Roman Catholic orders

flows.n: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath
flows.d: After allegations surfaced in 1977, the St John of God order transferred McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges; he was also convicted in New Zealand.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in New Zealand; Marylands School

flows.n: New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations
flows.d: New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care (2024) found the church transferred abusers to other ministries and recommended an investigation into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations. Numbers not stated.
flows.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, Whanaketia, July 2024, via EWTN/CNA

flows.n: Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy
flows.d: 1News reported in July 2020 that some of about 1,300 alleged clergy child abuse cases in Fiji involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand, and a survivor advocate said Fiji was a common destination for transferred clergy.
flows.cite: 1News, July 2020, via Wikipedia

flows.n: Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper
flows.d: After a 1994 abuse admission, the Archdiocese of Vancouver sent Cooper to a Long Island diocese, where he allegedly committed 'problems of a similar nature'.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Canada

flows.n: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince
flows.d: Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991; a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Canada

flows.n: Newfoundland → British Columbia: Brother Edward English
flows.d: After admitting in 1975 to molesting children at Mount Cashel, Edward English was transferred to British Columbia; a 2022 complaint alleges abuse at St. Thomas More Collegiate in Burnaby. A 2022 class action alleges six Christian Brothers who had abused in Newfoundland were later moved to teach at Vancouver College.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Catholic Church sexual abuse cases in Canada, citing CBC

flows.n: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
flows.d: After resigning amid clergy complaints in 2017, Zanchetta was given a post at the Vatican's patrimony office in December 2017; he was convicted in Argentina in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Gustavo Zanchetta

flows.n: Dominican Republic → Vatican: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski
flows.d: The nuncio was recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; he was laicised in 2014 and died in 2015 before a Vatican trial.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Józef Wesołowski

flows.n: Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil
flows.d: Suspended in May 2013, Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic; Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence and he was jailed for seven years in 2015.
flows.cite: Wikipedia, Józef Wesołowski

flows.n: Ballarat → Sydney: Fr Gerald Ridsdale
flows.d: After a dozen parish moves within the Ballarat diocese, Bishop Mulkearns, who knew of his offending by 1975, sent Ridsdale to the Catholic Enquiry Centre in Sydney in 1982; he was later convicted of abusing more than 70 children.
flows.cite: Royal Commission, Case Study 28, Dec 2017; The Courier

flows.n: United States → other countries: credibly accused clergy
flows.to: Other countries (destinations not itemised in source opened)
flows.size_note: 'More than 50' credibly accused US clergy moved to other countries (ProPublica/Houston Chronicle 2020); destination point is illustrative only
flows.d: A 2020 ProPublica and Houston Chronicle investigation found the church had moved more than 50 credibly accused US clergy to other countries after accusations surfaced. An earlier Dallas Morning News investigation found nearly half of 200 cases of accused priests abroad involved attempts to evade law enforcement. The destination point on the map is a placeholder; see notes.
flows.cite: ProPublica / Houston Chronicle, 2020; Dallas Morning News, 2004, via Wikipedia

notes:
SOURCING LIMITS IN THIS RUN: The shared web-search budget ran out after the first ~45 searches, and fetches to domains not already seen were blocked pending permission. Records after the first ~25 therefore rely mostly on Wikipedia (English, German, Spanish, French) summaries of primary sources; each such record's 'cite' names the underlying report and 'url' is the Wikipedia page actually opened. These should be upgraded to primary URLs in a later pass. Blocked URLs that were not read: vaticannews.va (Dec 2019 pontifical secret), theguardian.com (UN CRC 2014), vatican.va (2010 Ireland letter; 2018 Chile letter). Wikipedia rate-limited direct curl access.

UNVERIFIED / LEFT OUT: Switzerland (Univ. of Zurich, Sept 2023): commonly cited figures (1,002 cases, 510 accused, 921 victims) could NOT be confirmed from a page opened, so the record has no numbers. Portugal: 4,815 figure confirmed via Wikipedia summary only; other numbers (512 testimonies, 25 cases to prosecutors) not confirmed. Spain: Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo report (2024) and Spanish bishops' own count not opened. Cologne Gercke report (March 2021) could not be opened. Ireland Ryan Report: 2002 state-orders indemnity deal (18 orders) not confirmed. Mount Cashel first_report year (1975 police investigation) not confirmed, so omitted. Lawrence Murphy (Milwaukee deaf school) page not found. Michigan AG final report figures not obtained (only Dec 2019 interim). Cornwall Inquiry Catholic-specific findings not detailed.

NOT YET COVERED (leads): Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay (Urrutigoity / Bishop Livieres removal 2014), Guatemala, Costa Rica, Honduras, Puerto Rico (Arecibo), Uruguay; Papua New Guinea (only as a transfer destination); South Africa, Nigeria, DR Congo, Cameroon, Uganda, Ghana; South Korea, Japan, Sri Lanka, Hong Kong; Lithuania, Hungary, Slovakia, Denmark (17 cases by 2010 noted only in text); US cases of Joseph Jeyapaul (India<->Minnesota), Joseph Henn (Arizona->Rome, extradited 2019), Nicolás Aguilar Rivera (Mexico->Los Angeles 1987), Johannes Rivoire (Nunavut->France 1993), Eric Dejaeger flight to Belgium (1995) — all are documented cross-border cases to add as flows once sources can be opened. Also: Ireland Magdalene laundries / mother-and-baby homes (better in 'adoption'/'care' domain); Pennsylvania 2016 Altoona-Johnstown and Philadelphia 2005/2011 grand juries; New York, Colorado (2019 special master: 166 victims, 43 priests — unverified), Louisiana, Delaware, Oklahoma reports.

WHERE NATIONAL INQUIRIES HAVE NOT HAPPENED: No state or church-commissioned national inquiry was found for Brazil (largest Catholic population), Mexico (only a bishops' count), the Philippines (largest in Asia), Colombia, Argentina, Peru (only Sodalicio-specific), Italy (no official statistics; bishops said in 2012 priests had no duty to report to police), Poland (state commission exists but findings not obtained), India, or any African country (DR Congo, Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Angola etc.). African coverage here is limited to individual cases (Tanzania, Kenya, Mauritius, Malawi as a hiding place). The UN CRC (2014) noted that cases are 'hardly ever reported' because of a code of silence.

QUANTIFIED ESTIMATES (ESTIMATES, NOT FINDINGS): Holy See Archbishop Silvano Tomasi (2009) estimated 1.5–5% of clergy involved over 50 years. Holy See to UN Committee against Torture (2014): 3,420 cases investigated in the previous decade, 884 priests removed. BishopAccountability.org (as cited by Wikipedia): more than 3,000 civil lawsuits in the US and settlements over $3 billion by 2012. US dioceses paid about $4 billion to about 17,000 victims since the 1980s (Wikipedia summary). Fiji: about 1,300 alleged clergy abuse cases (1News 2020, as reported). France and Spain victim totals are survey-based estimates (marked in victims_note). Ireland 2018 list: over 1,300 clergy accused, 82 convicted (Wikipedia).

FIELD CONVENTIONS: Pell recorded as 'acquitted'. Zanchetta (adult seminarians) and Kevin Reynolds (false allegation, status 'disproved') kept because they show institutional transfer and false-claim patterns; Rupnik left out (adult victims only). Case-level 'officials' set true only where police/prosecutors/government were documented as obstructing or failing (Ferns, Murphy, Ballarat 1972 police, Mount Cashel, Smyth extradition, Ryan state inspection failures, Canadian residential schools).
